teaser: Two young diplomats, a shelf of science, and a smear on the floor that turns into a skull.
review_notes:
Ages: Dinteville 'in his 29th year' on the dagger sheath, de Selve 'in his 25th year' on the book edge; the lesson simplifies to 29 and 25.
Size about 207 x 209.5 cm, oil on oak.
Dinteville's letter calling himself the most melancholy ambassador (to his brother, 1533) is paraphrased.
Polyhedral sundial faces giving inconsistent readings: from National Gallery research.
Broken lute string and the missing flute: standard readings, not clearly visible at this image resolution.
Hymn book: Johann Walter's hymnal open at two Luther hymns.
Globe marked with Polisy, Dinteville's château.
Hanging theory (beside a doorway or on a staircase at Polisy) is a hypothesis.
Identification of the sitters by Mary F. S. Hervey, published 1900; National Gallery purchase 1890.
Floor based on the Cosmati pavement of Westminster Abbey.
Life dates: Dinteville 1504-1555, de Selve 1508/9-1541.
Best viewing point for the skull: from the right side of the painting, close to the wall.

lesson.text: Twenty-nine and twenty-five. Those are the ages of the two men in this painting, and Hans Holbein wrote both numbers into the picture so nobody would forget. They look older to us, with their furs, beards and stillness. In 1533 they were young, powerful, and stuck in London on a job neither of them enjoyed.

On the left stands Jean de Dinteville, ambassador of the King of France to the court of Henry VIII. On the right is his friend Georges de Selve, a bishop, who came to visit him that spring. The painting is almost square and about 2 meters on each side (roughly 6 feet 9 inches), so the figures are life size. In the gallery you meet them eye to eye.
Dinteville's age is written on something he is holding. Tap the object.

spots.title: The dagger
spots.text: The gold sheath in his right hand carries a Latin inscription with his age: 29. A heavy tassel hangs from it. He is the man of the court and the sword.

lesson.text: De Selve's number is quieter. It is written on the edge of the closed book under his right elbow: 25. A dagger for one, a book for the other. Holbein sets the friends up as two ways of living, the active and the thoughtful, then fills the space between them with everything their age was proud of knowing.

London, spring 1533: Henry VIII had just secretly married Anne Boleyn and was breaking with the Pope to do it. Dinteville's task was to watch the crisis for France. In a letter home he described himself as the most melancholy ambassador there ever was.

The piece of furniture between the two men has two levels, and its contents are sorted like a library. The upper shelf belongs to the sky: tools for mapping stars and telling time. The lower shelf belongs to life on the ground: geography, trade and music. Visit both.

lesson.title: Two shelves
lesson.text: Heaven above, earth below. Not everything on them is in working order.

spots.title: The star globe
spots.text: A blue globe of the heavens, its constellations drawn as animals and figures. Dinteville's elbow rests right beside it.

spots.title: The sundial
spots.text: A many-sided sundial with a little pointer on each face. Researchers who checked the shadows found that the faces do not agree with one another. Time is out of joint.

spots.title: The Earth
spots.text: A globe of the world with Europe turned toward us. Holbein wrote in the name of Polisy, the French village where Dinteville had his château and where the painting was going to hang.

spots.title: The lute
spots.text: Painted pointing toward us, the hardest angle to draw, as a show of skill. One of its strings has snapped. In a picture of diplomats, a broken string says that harmony has failed.

lesson.text: A snapped string, clocks that disagree: small alarms. Europe in 1533 was tearing apart between Catholics and the followers of Martin Luther, and both friends spent their careers trying to hold it together. The open hymn book beside the lute shows two hymns by Luther. Many read it as a wish that the churches might sing together again.

Now for the strangest thing in any portrait of the 1500s. A long gray-white smear floats above the floor, like driftwood or a stain. Everything else here is painted with razor precision, so Holbein did not slip. Try this: tilt your phone almost flat and squint along the smear from the right side of the screen. Or let the lines do it.
The smear has a direction, and a secret viewing point.

lines.label: The long axis
lines.text: The shape is pulled out hard along this slanting line, far beyond its natural length, and squashed thin across it.

lines.label: A skull
lines.text: Inside the outline are two dark eye sockets, a nose hole and a jaw, all dragged sideways. A picture distorted so that it only reads from one spot is called an anamorphosis.

lines.label: Where to stand
lines.text: Extend the axis to the right edge. A visitor standing there, close to the wall and looking back along the line, sees the stretch squeeze shut into a normal human skull.

lesson.text: A skull, in the middle of all that fur, silk and science. This is a memento mori, Latin for “remember that you will die”: a reminder slipped into a picture of success. The two men cannot see it from where they stand. Neither can you, from the front. You only find death when you step away from the usual point of view.

Nobody knows for certain how the painting was meant to hang. One theory places it beside a doorway or on a staircase in Dinteville's château, so that people passing would catch the skull out of the corner of an eye.

Death gets an answer, though, and it is even easier to overlook than the skull. Holbein tucked it at the very edge of the panel, half behind the green curtain, where almost no visitor thinks to check.
Something small and silver hides in one of the top corners. Which corner, and what is it?

spots.title: The crucifix
spots.text: A small silver figure of Christ on the cross, peeking out where the curtain ends. For these two believers it is the promise beyond the skull: death does not get the last word.

lesson.text: The picture reads in three layers. From the front: wealth, learning, friendship. From the side: death beneath it all. In the corner: hope behind it all.

Holbein packs that sermon in without spoiling the portrait. A German who had moved to London for work, he painted in oil on oak boards, building up thin, glassy layers. It is how he gets the soft fur lining of Dinteville's coat, the pink satin sleeve with its hard highlights, and the knotted wool of the carpet. Each material answers the light in its own way.
Holbein painted Turkish carpets like the one on the upper shelf so often, and so exactly, that rug experts now call the whole type “Holbein carpets.”

The painting went home to France with Dinteville and slipped out of sight for centuries. By the time the National Gallery in London bought it in 1890, nobody remembered who the two men were. A researcher named Mary Hervey dug through the archives and gave them their names back in 1900.

spots.title: The medal
spots.text: On Dinteville's gold chain hangs the badge of the Order of Saint Michael, the highest honor a French king could give.

spots.title: Aged 25
spots.text: The closed book under de Selve's elbow. Its edge carries the Latin note of his age, the quiet partner of the number on the dagger.

spots.title: The math book
spots.text: A printed arithmetic manual for merchants, propped half open. The page on show deals with division, a pointed word in a divided Europe.

spots.title: The hymn book
spots.text: Music and German words, painted so exactly that the two hymns can be identified. Both are by Martin Luther.

spots.title: The flutes
spots.text: A leather case of flutes sits by the hymn book. One flute is missing from the set: another instrument that can no longer play in tune with the rest.

spots.title: The bishop's gown
spots.text: A long dark robe of patterned silk, no weapon, hands closed. A churchman's restraint next to Dinteville's pink satin and swagger.

spots.title: The floor
spots.text: The inlaid stone pattern copies a real one: the medieval pavement before the high altar of Westminster Abbey in London, where English monarchs are crowned.

lesson.text: Twenty-nine and twenty-five. Dinteville lived to about fifty. De Selve died eight years after posing, at about thirty-two. The skull was right, as it always is. But the two friends are still standing there in their best clothes, and visitors still step sideways, every day, to find what the two of them could not see.

quiz.question: Where did Holbein write Dinteville's age?
quiz.explanation: The gold sheath in his hand carries the inscription.

quiz.question: What does the upper shelf hold?
options: Instruments for studying the sky and time
quiz.explanation: The top shelf belongs to the heavens: a star globe and sundials.

quiz.question: What is an anamorphosis?
options: An image distorted so it reads correctly from one viewpoint only
A painting made on oak boards
quiz.explanation: The skull only looks right when seen from the side, along its axis.

quiz.question: What does the broken lute string suggest?
quiz.explanation: A snapped string was a sign of discord, fitting a Europe split by religion.

quiz.question: What is half hidden behind the curtain in the top left corner?
quiz.explanation: A small crucifix answers the skull with a promise of salvation.

quiz.question: What real place does the floor copy?
quiz.explanation: The pattern follows the medieval pavement in Westminster Abbey.

facts.text: The two sitters were always known by name, from 1533 to today.
facts.explanation: Their identities were forgotten and only recovered by Mary Hervey in 1900.

facts.text: The skull looks normal when the painting is seen from the side.
facts.explanation: Looking along its long axis squeezes the stretched shape back into a skull.

facts.text: Both men in the painting were over fifty when they posed.
facts.explanation: They were 29 and 25, as the inscriptions say.
